Chacunda gizzard shad, Anodontostoma chacunda, is a clupeiform fish widely distributed across coastal and estuarine waters of the Indo-West Pacific. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum body size of 22 cm [Li = 22 cm] in total length, an ultimate dimension that places it among the moderately sized members of the family Dorosomatidae. Foraging primarily on phytoplankton and detritus, the shad exhibits a filter-feeding mode typical of gizzard shads, with gill raker morphology adapted to retain fine particulate matter. Reproductive biology in this species is strongly influenced by seasonal monsoonal cycles, with spawning peaks coinciding with periods of elevated turbidity and phytoplankton blooms. Mature adults migrate into shallow, brackish inshore zones to release their eggs, which are semi-buoyant and drift with tidal currents. The species is iteroparous, with individuals capable of spawning multiple times within a single breeding season given adequate resource availability. Comparative studies with congeneric species suggest that Anodontostoma chacunda exhibits a moderately fast life-history strategy, balancing relatively high fecundity against a modest adult body size, a pattern typical of tropical clupeiforms inhabiting productive continental shelf environments.

At the time of reproductive maturation, females reach a total length of 14.1 cm [Lp = 14.1 cm], corresponding to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. This length at puberty represents approximately 64 percent of the species' ultimate length, a value consistent with the life-history patterns observed in other dorosomatid shads from tropical estuaries. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals that oocyte development proceeds asynchronously, indicating batch spawning capability over an extended breeding season. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 29 grams [Wwp = 29 grams], a body mass that reflects the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gamete production. Energy allocation toward reproductive effort increases markedly after this size threshold is crossed, with gravid females exhibiting a pronounced distension of the abdominal cavity due to developing oocytes. Field-caught pubertal individuals display a gonadosomatic index that rises sharply during the pre-monsoon period, suggesting that photoperiod and temperature act as proximate cues for reproductive activation in this tropical clupeiform.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], eggs of Anodontostoma chacunda complete their incubation period within 3 days [ab = 3 days], yielding newly hatched yolk-sac larvae that are entirely endotrophic during the initial phase of development. The short incubation duration is typical of warm-water clupeiforms and is linked to rapid cleavage and gastrulation rates at elevated temperatures. At the moment of eclosion, each prolarva emerges with a wet weight of 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 0.95 mm and reflecting the modest volume of yolk reserves provisioned by the female. This small birth mass imposes a narrow window for exogenous feeding onset, as yolk reserves are depleted rapidly at the prevailing temperature. The temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] also governs the pace of yolk-sac resorption, mouth opening, and retinal differentiation, all of which must occur before the point of no return is reached. Survival during the early larval phase is thus strongly contingent on the synchrony between yolk depletion and the availability of suitable planktonic prey in the surrounding water column.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Anodontostoma chacunda under natural conditions is 5 years [am = 5 years], a value obtained from otolith-based age estimation studies conducted across multiple populations in Southeast Asian coastal waters at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that of other small-bodied dorosomatid shads, which typically exhibit life spans ranging from three to seven years depending on local environmental conditions and predation pressure. Within this five-year window, adult fish grow rapidly during the first two years before approaching an asymptotic body mass. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals is 112.4 grams [Wwi = 112.4 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the value predicted from the length-weight relationship derived for this species. Senescence in older age classes is evidenced by reduced condition factors, increased incidence of parasitic infestation, and diminished gonadal output during the final spawning seasons. Natural mortality rates are highest among early larvae and spawning adults, the latter reflecting the energetic cost of repeated reproductive events in a warm, productive estuarine environment.

Fecundity in Anodontostoma chacunda ranges from 297457 to 1144871 eggs per reproductive event, with the number of oocytes released increasing linearly with female body size and condition. At a water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], gravid females produce eggs continuously over the breeding season, yielding an estimated annual reproductive output of approximately 700,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 700,000 eggs per year], a rate sustained only when thermal and trophic conditions are optimal. This high fecundity is an adaptation to the high egg and larval mortality characteristic of turbid, predator-rich estuarine environments, where only a minute fraction of offspring survive to recruitment. Comparative analyses indicate that the reproductive output of Anodontostoma chacunda exceeds that of many temperate clupeiforms of equivalent body size, reflecting the selective pressures imposed by the warm, stochastic environments of tropical coastal zones. Life-history theory predicts that such high fecundity should be balanced by relatively low investment per offspring, a prediction consistent with the small egg diameter and modest larval size at hatching observed in this species.
